part_title: Secure GenAI Architecture, Least Privilege and Data Masking

scenes.title: Security, Identity, and Compliance
scenes.narration: Begin by following the GenAI application architecture across the centre. A human user or application sends a request through API Gateway, where identity and request policy checks begin. Lambda validates inputs, builds prompts and applies application permissions before it invokes Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock supplies the foundation model and applicable safety controls, while S3 holds approved application data, prompts or outputs with restricted access. The three headings around this picture describe distinct responsibilities. Identity answers who is making the call and what they are permitted to do. Protection means encryption, content controls and safe data handling at every hop. Evidence means keeping useful logs and traces so administrators can explain which principal invoked a model, when and with what outcome. The key is that security is not implemented by one service at the end of the pipeline. A model endpoint can be protected but still receive sensitive information from an overprivileged Lambda function. Review each trust boundary, require authentication and authorisation, encrypt data in transit and at rest, and retain only the audit information you need.

scenes.title: Principle of least privilege
scenes.narration: This slide puts one Lambda execution role at the centre of a permissions decision. On the allowed side, the function needs to invoke a specific Bedrock model and read objects under a particular S3 prompts prefix. On the blocked side, the same function should not write arbitrary S3 objects, change DynamoDB records or create IAM users. The policy example below narrows allowed actions to bedrock InvokeModel and s3 GetObject on explicit resources. Look carefully at the object ARN ending in prompts slash star: that prefix restriction matters because a broad S3 wildcard would expose unrelated data. Similarly, model resource restrictions should match the actual model or inference profile being invoked. In AWS IAM, permissions not explicitly granted are normally denied, while an explicit Deny overrides even another Allow. The engineering rationale is blast-radius reduction: if the function is compromised, an attacker inherits only its necessary capabilities rather than administrator permissions. Start by listing the actual API calls the workload requires, narrow the resources, validate the policy with tests and monitor access-denied errors for unintended gaps.

scenes.title: Data masking and anonymization
scenes.narration: Compare the customer-support record on the left with the safe model input on the right. The original record contains a person's name, email address, phone number and an account-access issue. The masking gateway between them detects sensitive fields before the data is submitted to the model. The transformed record replaces the name with a pseudonymous customer identifier, partially masks the email and hides most of the phone number while retaining the support issue. The point is to preserve useful context without sending unnecessary personal information into a model prompt or logging system. Notice that pseudonymisation is not always irreversible anonymisation: if a secure mapping can recover the original person, the data may still be personal data and requires protection. Free-text fields can also contain card details or identifiers, so field-level masking alone is insufficient. Build a policy for both structured and unstructured input, and test whether protected values can leak through generated responses. Data minimisation complements encryption and IAM; neither of those controls removes sensitive content from a prompt automatically.

scenes.title: Data Masking Techniques
scenes.narration: This slide compares four techniques that are easy to confuse. Redaction replaces an entire sensitive value with a placeholder, for example showing redacted instead of a name or phone number. Tokenization substitutes a generated token for a card number, while a protected token vault may allow an authorised system to restore the original. Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with consistent substitute values such as User one zero four two, preserving the ability to link related records. Generalization replaces a precise value with a broader category, for instance an age band or income range. Follow each example table to see what information remains useful and what identifying detail disappears. The right choice depends on the downstream task: an AI assistant may only need an age category, while a payment processor may require controlled token recovery. A hashed or pseudonymous ID is not necessarily anonymous if it can be linked to a person. Keep any mapping keys or vaults isolated, and evaluate whether combinations of supposedly harmless fields could still identify a user.

scenes.title: Salted password hashing
scenes.narration: Follow the registration path at the top. When a user creates a password, the application generates a unique random salt and passes the password through a password-hashing function that incorporates that salt. The database stores the salt and resulting hash, not the original password. Now follow the login path below: the application retrieves the stored parameters, hashes the candidate password using the same salt and algorithm, and compares the result securely. The benefit is that two users choosing the same password should still have different stored hashes. Salts also defeat precomputed rainbow tables that rely on unsalted password hashes. Importantly, a salt does not need to be kept secret; uniqueness is its main purpose. The diagram mentions bcrypt and Argon2, which are designed for password hashing. For real authentication systems, use a well-supported adaptive password-hashing configuration rather than ordinary fast SHA two five six alone. This slows offline guessing attacks and supports future parameter upgrades. A password hash protects stored credentials but does not replace MFA, safe reset flows or protection against credential phishing.
